teaser.text: SSE plc is an energy-infrastructure company: it owns the wires, power stations and customer businesses that make electricity usable. A pound comes in when someone pays for network access, electricity, availability or an energy service, and goes out on construction, fuel, maintenance, financing and tax.

stock.title: SSE stock forecast
stock.meta_description: SSE's weighted scenario points higher if network investment and renewable growth become earnings per share, with cash and valuation risks in view.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for SSE, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: Earnings provide the main operating bridge, but the forecast keeps a deduction between adjusted EPS and reported earnings. FY26 adjusted net income was £1,758.5m, while reported net income was £1,208.7m because of wind impairments and restructuring. The base earnings row rises from £1,832m in October 2027 to £2,355m in October 2029. It assumes adjusted EPS of £1.80 in the first year and £2.15 in the last, supported by network investment and renewable growth. The bear row ends at £1,639m because delays and cost pressure persist; the bull reaches £2,819m as commissioning and output improve. The base starts within FY27 guidance of £1.68–£1.93 adjusted EPS and remains below the £2.25–£2.50 FY30 target before that year ends.

blocks.heading: How much cash does SSE really make?

paragraphs.text: After construction spending and lease payments, free cash flow was negative. That can be sensible during expansion, but only if the new networks and generation assets eventually produce adequate cash returns. SSE’s “real free cash flow” goes further by subtracting share-based compensation. The shares require no immediate cash payment, but they are still an economic cost to existing owners.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for SSE today?

paragraphs.text: SSE’s share price asks investors to fund heavy construction spending before the resulting earnings arrive. At 2521.00p on 15 October 2026, its shares were worth £30,778.0m, while enterprise value was £38,899.6m. Enterprise value estimates the operating business for shareholders and lenders together: it adds debt and debt-like claims to the shares and subtracts cash. The £8,121.6m gap is therefore a valuation bridge, not automatically SSE’s net debt. SSE’s own adjusted net debt and hybrid capital was £10.1bn at March 2026, using a different definition and date.

dividend.meta_description: SSE's dividend is 68.7p per share, cash flow was negative in FY26, and management guides to 5–10% annual growth.
dividend.opening: SSE's latest dividend was 68.7p per share; the forecast shows 72p rising to 80p in the base case. Free cash flow was negative in FY26, so the business did not cover the dividend from free cash flow.
dividend.closing: The full memo also examines SSE's business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: How much does SSE pay per share?

paragraphs.text: Dividends grow from 72p to 80p in the base case, remain at 69p in the bear case and reach 91p in the bull case. The base applies the low end of SSE’s stated 5–10% policy, while the bull applies the high end. The bear case holds the latest 68.7p dividend flat because capital spending exceeded operating cash and free cash flow was negative in FY26. The flat assumption is cautious rather than catastrophic: the historic reset from 96.7p to 60.0p shows that a cut remains possible if funding deteriorates.

paragraphs.text: Management guides to adjusted EPS of 168–193p for FY2027 and targets 225–250p for FY2030. It plans about £5.0bn of FY2027 capital investment and guides to net debt/EBITDA no higher than 4.5x. It expects annual dividend growth of 5–10% through FY2028.

The bear probability would rise if FY27 results show missed adjusted EPS guidance, weaker margins or transmission overruns. Higher borrowing costs during FY27–FY30 would further weaken project returns, dividend growth and the valuation multiple.

blocks.heading: What is SSE's dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: Revenue fell from £12,490.7m in FY2023 to £10,186.5m in FY2026, while the company’s own real free cash flow swung from positive 11.7% of revenue in FY2024 to negative 10.8% in FY2026. Diluted EPS fell from 156.50p in FY2024 to 105.40p in FY2026. At 2521.00p on 15 October 2026, the valuation carried a 23.9x trailing P/E, a negative 3.5% free cash flow yield and a 2.7% dividend yield.

blocks.heading: How have SSE's results changed over the last eight reported periods?

paragraphs.text: SSE reports full financial statements half-yearly, so the eight periods in the comparison are six-month periods rather than quarters. In the latest March half-year, revenue was lower than a year earlier but operating income, net income and diluted EPS were higher. That combination shows why sales are a weak scorecard when the business mix is changing.

Cash also improved, yet capital spending increased and free cash flow remained negative. The company was still funding construction faster than its operations paid for it. Seasonal earnings matter too: the March half-year is naturally different from the September half-year, so a change should be compared with the same season before it is called a trend.

blocks.heading: What should investors watch in SSE's next results?

paragraphs.text: The 18 November 2026 interim results will test whether networks are reducing SSE’s earnings seasonality. A larger regulated contribution should make the first half more substantial, but winter weather, power prices and plant availability still matter. First-half earnings alone will not settle the full-year outcome.

Dogger Bank A should be substantially commissioned by the end of 2026. The important questions are how much capacity operates reliably, what work remains and whether spending has risen. At Dogger Bank B, installed turbines must translate into operating output rather than merely a higher installation count.
